key_facts: **Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)** is a necrotising vasculitis of **medium-sized arteries**.
Skin: tender subcutaneous nodules, **livedo racemosa**, ulcers, digital ischaemia; cutaneous PAN may be skin-limited.
Systemic PAN: hypertension, renal infarcts, mononeuritis multiplex, abdominal pain, weight loss; **ANCA negative**.
Associated with hepatitis B; deep incisional biopsy of a nodule needed.
Specialist treatment: steroids ± cyclophosphamide; antivirals for HBV-PAN.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **PAN** is a **necrotising arteritis of medium (and small) muscular arteries**, **without glomerulonephritis** or vasculitis of arterioles/capillaries/venules, and **not associated with ANCA** (CHCC 2012). It is rare (~2–30 per million), with a peak at 40–60 years. Forms:

ul: **systemic PAN** — idiopathic, or **HBV-associated** (now rare in vaccinated populations), HCV, HIV, hairy-cell leukaemia, **DADA2** (adenosine deaminase-2 deficiency, especially childhood or young-onset with strokes)
**cutaneous (single-organ) PAN** — skin ± local muscle/nerve/joint, a chronic relapsing course, rarely becoming systemic.

sub: Rare; adults 40–60; children with cutaneous PAN after streptococcal infection.

ul: **"Normal ANCA excludes vasculitis"**: PAN is ANCA-negative.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: PAN inflames and destroys the **walls of medium arteries**, causing aneurysms and infarcts.

mech.t: Hepatitis B immune complexes or unknown triggers.
Fibrinoid necrosis of the full arterial wall at the dermo-subcutaneous junction.
Weakened walls balloon (microaneurysms); thrombosis causes infarction.
Patchy arterial blockage gives broken livedo, nodules and ulcers.

blocks: Immune complexes (e.g. HBsAg–antibody in HBV-PAN, typically within 6–12 months of infection) or other triggers cause **segmental transmural fibrinoid necrosis** at arterial branch points → **microaneurysms**, thrombosis, stenosis → **infarction** of the organs supplied:

ul: **renal arteries → renovascular hypertension, infarcts (not GN)**
vasa nervorum → **mononeuritis multiplex**
mesenteric → abdominal pain/bowel infarction
testes → orchitis
coronary arteries
skin → nodules, livedo racemosa, ulcers, digital gangrene.

histo: Necrotising arteritis of medium vessels in deep dermis/subcutis; deep biopsy required.

ul: **Systemic:** fever, **weight loss**, myalgia, arthralgia; **mononeuritis multiplex/polyneuropathy** (foot/wrist drop, patchy numbness); **hypertension**; renal impairment; abdominal pain after meals (mesenteric angina), GI bleed; **testicular pain**; MI/heart failure; stroke (DADA2).

**Skin (~25–60%):** **tender subcutaneous nodules (0.5–2 cm) along arteries** of the lower legs/thighs; **livedo racemosa** (feet, legs); **punched-out ulcers** (D02 — sensitive); digital ischaemia; "starburst" livedo around nodules.

**Cutaneous PAN:** recurrent painful nodules ± livedo/ulcers on the lower legs, with local myalgia/arthralgia/neuropathy in the same limb. Triggers: **streptococcal infection** (children), IBD, HBV/HCV, **minocycline** (drug-induced cPAN — link to the [drug eruption](condition:drug-eruption-approach) notes/acne). ANCA negative; usually no internal organ involvement.

**No single blood test**. Diagnosis combines clinical features, exclusion of mimics, **histology** and **angiography**: **ESR/CRP** raised; normocytic anaemia; leucocytosis; thrombocytosis; **ANCA negative** (positive ANCA points to MPA/GPA/EGPA); **Hepatitis B (HBsAg, HBeAg, HBV DNA) and C**, HIV, cryoglobulins, complement, ANA, APL antibodies, blood cultures; **Urinalysis** (no active sediment — red-cell casts suggest GN, so not PAN); **ADA2 activity/genetics** in young patients
**Biopsy:** deep **incisional skin biopsy of a nodule to subcutis** (medium artery with fibrinoid necrosis; DIF non-specific), or **muscle/sural nerve biopsy** guided by symptoms/EMG.
**Imaging:** **CT/MR angiography or catheter angiography** — **microaneurysms** and stenoses of renal/mesenteric/hepatic arteries ("arteriographic abnormality").

**ACR 1990 classification criteria (≥3 of 10):** weight loss ≥4 kg; livedo reticularis; testicular pain/tenderness; myalgias/weakness/leg tenderness; mono- or polyneuropathy; diastolic BP >90 mmHg; raised urea/creatinine (BUN >40 mg/dL or creatinine >1.5 mg/dL); HBV markers; arteriographic abnormality; biopsy showing neutrophils in a small/medium artery wall. These are **classification** criteria, not diagnostic.

**French Vasculitis Study Group predictive items (Henegar 2008; course list):** positive — **HBsAg+, arteriographic abnormalities, mono/polyneuropathy**; negative — **ANCA, asthma, ENT signs, glomerulopathy, cryoglobulinaemia**.
**Cutaneous vs systemic PAN:**

head: Cutaneous PAN
Systemic PAN
rows: Kidney (renovascular), nerves (mononeuritis multiplex), gut, heart, testes
NSAIDs, colchicine, dapsone, topical/intralesional/oral steroids, methotrexate, IVIg; penicillin if strep

ul: **Severity — revised Five-Factor Score (FFS 2011)** for PAN: age >65, cardiac insufficiency, GI involvement, renal insufficiency (creatinine ≥150 µmol/L). Each = 1 point; ≥1 point = worse prognosis → cyclophosphamide added.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses
blocks: ANCA-associated vasculitis (MPA — GN and lung haemorrhage; GPA; EGPA — asthma, eosinophilia), cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis (HCV), SLE/RA vasculitis, **infective endocarditis** (emboli, aneurysms — blood cultures), **antiphospholipid syndrome**, cholesterol emboli, segmental arterial mediolysis, fibromuscular dysplasia, Buerger's disease, calciphylaxis, lymphoma, EN/panniculitis (the [drug eruption](condition:drug-eruption-approach) notes see *Livedo reticularis vs livedo racemosa* for nodules), DADA2.

sections.title: Management

ul: **Systemic PAN → urgent rheumatology/renal admission.** BP 160/100 with raised creatinine, neuropathy and necrotic ulcers is organ-threatening.

**Non-HBV systemic PAN (ACR/VF 2021; EULAR):** Induction: **high-dose glucocorticoids** (e.g. IV methylprednisolone pulses then prednisolone ~1 mg/kg/day, max ~60 mg, tapering over months); **Add cyclophosphamide** for severe disease (FFS ≥1, neuropathy, renal, GI, cardiac involvement); Maintenance: azathioprine or methotrexate (total ~18 months); Supportive: **BP control** (ACE-i/ARB for renin-mediated hypertension, with care if renal artery stenosis); PJP prophylaxis (co-trimoxazole) on cyclophosphamide; bone protection; gastroprotection; Steroid Emergency Card; vaccines (no live); fertility counselling before cyclophosphamide

**HBV-associated PAN (the case) — different strategy:** **Antiviral therapy** (entecavir or tenofovir; lamivudine historically) via hepatology; A **short course of glucocorticoids** (e.g. ~2 weeks, to control life-threatening inflammation) and **plasma exchange** to clear immune complexes, until HBeAg seroconversion; **Avoid prolonged steroids and cyclophosphamide**, which boost HBV replication and risk fulminant hepatitis (Guillevin regimen); Notify/contact-trace and vaccinate household and sexual contacts (UKHSA); This differs from the "prednisolone 6 months + cyclophosphamide 12 months" approach in a student answer, which suits severe **non-HBV** PAN

**Cutaneous PAN:** NSAIDs/colchicine/dapsone → short steroid courses → methotrexate/azathioprine; treat strep (penicillin prophylaxis in children with recurrent strep-triggered cPAN); stop minocycline.

blocks: Recognition, bloods (incl. hepatitis serology, urinalysis, BP), referral, and post-discharge support: shared-care monitoring of azathioprine/methotrexate (FBC/LFT/U&E schedules), PJP prophylaxis checks, steroid card, vaccines (inactivated only), BP management. Induction therapy is specialist.

refer.t: Foot drop or new numbness, severe abdominal pain or testicular pain with nodules or livedo: **urgent** referral for systemic PAN.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Foot drop or new numbness, severe abdominal pain or testicular pain with nodules or livedo: **urgent** referral for systemic PAN.

blocks: Hypertension + renal impairment; mononeuritis multiplex (foot/wrist drop); post-prandial abdominal pain/GI bleeding; testicular pain; chest pain; digital ischaemia/gangrene; nodules + livedo racemosa + ulcers; HBsAg positive with vasculitic features → urgent/same day.

ul: Renal failure, hypertension, bowel infarction, stroke, neuropathy.
Cutaneous PAN is chronic but benign; systemic PAN is serious but often remits with treatment.

pearls: "**Nodules + livedo + neuropathy + hypertension, ANCA negative → think PAN, and check hepatitis B.**"
PAN **spares glomeruli**. Haematuria with red-cell casts points to ANCA vasculitis.
Hepatitis B serology **before** starting steroids/immunosuppressants for any vasculitis (reactivation risk) — this applies to rituximab especially.

quiz.q: When should you think of Polyarteritis nodosa (systemic & cutaneous)?
quiz.a: Tender subcutaneous nodules along vessels, livedo racemosa and painful ulcers on the lower legs.
Necrotising inflammation of medium-sized arteries; hepatitis B, streptococcal infection and some drugs are triggers.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: BP, urine, renal function, hepatitis B/C serology; deep (incisional) biopsy; refer to rheumatology/dermatology; specialist immunosuppression.
Systemic PAN: mononeuritis multiplex, abdominal pain, testicular pain, hypertension, renal infarcts.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Foot drop or new numbness, severe abdominal pain or testicular pain with nodules or livedo: **urgent** referral for systemic PAN.
